title: Latency vs Fidelity tradeoff lab demo for Aurora Health
summary: Redwood team demoed Optimize console and a small lab comparing INT8 and FP8 profiles on Aurora's conversational workload. Focus on latency vs fidelity tradeoffs, rollout strategy using canary/prefix caching, and recommended benchmarks. Customer concerned about HIPAA data handling and reproducible evals. Agreed next steps: Redwood to share sandbox access, detailed benchmark spreadsheet, and security whitepaper.
action_items: Maya Chen | share benchmark spreadsheet and sample prompts | 2026-03-02
Liam O'Connor | provision sandbox cluster and invite Aurora engineers | 2026-03-04
Ellen Yu | provide representative prompt set and acceptance criteria | 2026-03-03
transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2026-02-27 15:00 UTC
- Duration: 52 minutes
- Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Liam (Redwood SE), Priya (Product), Diego (Optimize), Sofia (Aurora ML), Mark (CTO), Ellen (Platform), Chris (Security)

Summary / Topics covered (auto):
- Quick Optimize console tour, quant profiles INT8/FP8
- Latency/fidelity lab results on a 2k token avg convo
- Rollout and canary strategies, KV/prefix cache behavior
- Security and data residency brief Q&A

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: ok hi everyone, thanks for joining, i'm Maya from Redwood, liam and diego and priya are here to run through the Optimize walkthrough — we'll show an example lab comparing int8 and fp8 profiles on a conversational model that matches a healthcare support bot workload.
[00:22] Sofia: hey thanks, excited. quick note — our main constraints are 200ms p95 for short queries, and clinical-fidelity for triage responses, so we need to see quality numbers.
[00:40] Liam: great, we'll start with an overview, then run live console benchmarks. note, some of the numbers in the console are from our internal runner, you'll want to reproduce with your prompts.
[01:02] Diego: jumping in — Optimize has prebuilt quant profiles. INT8 tends to drop some rare-entity fidelity; FP8 keeps better token-level scores but costs more and adds a little latency. we'll show you both.
[01:25] Mark: can you give ballpark costs? also we have to confirm HIPAA handling — how does sandbox handle PHI?
[01:38] Priya: quick answer on PHI — sandbox can be deployed in your VPC (private mode) and we support KMS and audit logs; we'll send the security whitepaper, but chris you can ask detailed Qs after the demo.
[01:55] Chris: yeah i'll follow up. also curious about deterministic evals — how do we measure quality consistently?
[02:10] Liam: we recommend a fixed prompt set, n-gram and embedding-based similarity, and a human-eval sample. we'll upload a sample metric sheet.

[02:35] Live console walkthrough:
[02:35] Diego: ok opening Optimize -> Quant Profiles. here you can select model variant, target latency SLO, and run a profile sweep. im starting a sweep between INT8 and FP8 on the 'oracle-med-conv' model we preloaded. pardon the typo in the model name, it's 'oracl-med' locally.
[03:04] Diego: first chart shows throughput vs latency. INT8 gives ~1.9x throughput improvement and median token-latency drop of ~40% on our bench. however in the quality panel we see a BLEURT-ish metric dip of about 2.8 points for edge-case clinical prompts.
[03:38] Sofia: that's concerning — when you say edge-case, what examples?
[03:44] Diego: e.g. rare medication interactions, long context (>1k tokens) where quantization noise affects retrieval-like steps. the model hallucinated a dosage in one seed.
[03:56] Liam: to mitigate we recommend hybrid policy: INT8 for short tokens/prefixes and FP8 for the final response window, or fallback to FP8 when the query hits certain triggers (entities, medical tokens). the console lets you set rules.
[04:20] Maya: can you show the rule config?
[04:23] Diego: sure — Policies -> Precision Routing -> create rule. trigger: entity-detected("medication|dosage|allergy") -> route to fp8; else int8. you can also set a cost cap so it only uses fp8 for 3% of requests.
[04:45] Ellen: how does the KV cache interplay? if you cache prefixes, will int8 still be okay?
[04:52] Liam: good question. prefix/KV caching preserves past key/values; if you cache a prefix that was encoded in FP8 and later decode in INT8-ish runtime there can be mismatch noise. recommended: pin precision for the KV cache or normalize cache keys per-precision, Optimize has an option to namespace caches per-profile.
[05:18] Diego: showing the benchmarking tab — i'm running a 1k-req bench now, results updating... p50 p95 p99 latency charts, token-cost per request, and fidelity delta versus FP32 baseline in the same table.
[05:42] [crosstalk] Mark: sorry did you say p95 numbers?
[05:45] Diego: yes, p95 for INT8 was 180ms in our lab, FP8 was 230ms; FP32 baseline 300ms. quality delta: INT8 -2.8 BLEURT, FP8 -0.9 BLEURT. these are illustrative — for your prompts we'll run the same.
[06:07] Sofia: what about streaming and partial responses? our front-end streams token-by-token.
[06:15] Liam: streaming latency is mostly first-token latency + token generation. INT8 helps with throughput but first-token sometimes depends on kernel compile and token-decode path. we recommend warming kernels and using persistent engines in Dedicated.
[06:35] Maya: quick pause — note that on Hosted we can do warm pools; on Dedicated you have persistent GPUs for even lower cold starts.
[06:45] Chris: for compliance, we need logs of model version and precision used per request. do you expose that in audit logs?
[06:52] Priya: yes, every request record includes model_version, quant_profile, routing decision, and TTI/TTR timings in the audit logs. those can be shipped to your SIEM via syslog/S3.

[07:10] Deep-dive: fidelity metrics
[07:10] Diego: ok here's the fidelity tab — we show multiple metrics: BLEURT, ROUGE-L, embedding-similarity to golden answers, and a human-fidelity thumbs sample. for medical domain we prefer embedding-sim + constrained entity match.
[07:30] Sofia: can we threshold entity-match? e.g. never accept new dosage suggestions unless entity match >= 0.98?
[07:38] Diego: you can. Optimize supports rule-based gating: if entity-confidence < threshold, fallback to pass-through to clinician queue or to FP8.

[07:55] Live example prompt run (short):
[07:55] Diego: running sample prompt "patient reports severe headache after starting drug X, also taking blood thinner". INT8 response: (displayed) — contains a mild hallucinated interaction name. FP8 response: (displayed) — correctly lists known interaction and cites source.
[08:25] Sofia: ok clear why FP8 helps there.

[08:40] Latency SLOs & rollout strategy
[08:40] Liam: approach we recommend: 1) run offline sweep on your prompt set, 2) pick profile that meets quality thresholds and deploy as canary to 5-10% traffic, 3) monitor fidelity and error rates for 48-72h, escalate to FP8 for failing segments, 4) expand if stable.
[09:05] Maya: cost controls — set usage caps and automated rollback if fidelity drops. Console has automatic rollback based on eval-suite regressions.
[09:16] Mark: how granular are rollbacks? route-level, user-level?
[09:20] Priya: route-level and tag-level; you can annotate by team or patient type.

[09:34] Benchmark reproducibility and dev workflow
[09:34] Diego: we pushed a small benchmarking repo and runner (link shared in chat). it can replay requests, record traces, compute metrics. use it in sandbox to reproduce exactly.
[09:50] Sofia: please send the runner.
[09:52] Maya: will do, action item to attach.

[10:05] Security Q&A quick notes
[10:05] Chris: if we run in your hosted environment, do you allow log redaction? we can't store PHI.
[10:13] Priya: yes automatic redaction hooks, or exclude logs entirely. VPC/private install gives you full control.
[10:20] Chris: how about key management?
[10:22] Priya: KMS/HSM integration supported, customer-provided keys in Private mode.

[10:35] Follow-up: sandbox and pilot details
[10:35] Liam: for the sandbox we'll provision a small dedicated cluster with both FP8 and INT8 profiles available, we'll invite your SREs. expected setup time 2 business days after signoff.
[10:47] Ellen: that sounds good. we'll prepare a 500-2000 prompt set and acceptance criteria.
[10:51] Sofia: timeline — we want a pilot in 2 weeks if possible.
[10:54] Maya: we can aim for that pending sandbox creds and prompts.

[11:05] Recap & next steps (wrap)
[11:05] Maya: recap: 1) we'll share benchmark spreadsheet and runner, 2) provision sandbox cluster, 3) send security whitepaper and SOC2 artifacts, 4) schedule 30-min pilot kickoff. owners and due dates in action items.
[11:22] Mark: thanks everyone, very helpful.
[11:26] Sofia: thanks, looking forward to the sandbox.
[11:30] End of call.

Notes on transcription: some proper nouns may be slightly off (model name abbreviations), occasional overlap and filler words kept.
